description: Stage-1 RAG chat test set. Each question has one expected document, a verbatim evidence passage from that document (used to score retrieval), and a key fact the answer must contain (any alias counts).

questions.question: What is the maximum line length the Python style guide recommends for code?
questions.evidence: Limit all lines to a maximum of 79 characters.

questions.question: How long should lines be for docstrings and comments under the style guide?
questions.evidence: (docstrings or comments), the line length should be limited to 72 characters.

questions.question: How many spaces should be used per indentation level?
questions.evidence: Use 4 spaces per indentation level.

questions.question: For new code, should a line break come before or after a binary operator, and whose style is that?
questions.evidence: In Python code, it is permissible to break before or after a binary operator, as long as the convention is consistent locally. For new code Knuth's style is suggested.

questions.question: How many blank lines should surround top-level function and class definitions?
questions.evidence: Surround top-level function and class definitions with two blank lines.

questions.question: How should comparisons to singletons like None be written?
questions.evidence: Comparisons to singletons like None should always be done with ``is`` or ``is not``, never the equality operators.

questions.question: How are module-level constants supposed to be named?
questions.evidence: Constants are usually defined on a module level and written in all capital letters with underscores separating words.

questions.question: What source file encoding should code in the core Python distribution use?
questions.evidence: Code in the core Python distribution should always use UTF-8, and should not have an encoding declaration.

questions.question: When is it acceptable to use a bare except clause?
questions.evidence: If the exception handler will be printing out or logging the traceback; at least the user will be aware that an error has occurred.

questions.question: What kind of quotes should always be used around docstrings?
questions.evidence: For consistency, always use ``"""triple double quotes"""`` around docstrings.

questions.question: What quoting should a docstring use if it contains backslashes?
questions.evidence: Use ``r"""raw triple double quotes"""`` if you use any backslashes in your docstrings.

questions.question: Should a one-line docstring describe the function ("Returns the pathname") or phrase its effect as a command?
questions.evidence: It prescribes the function or method's effect as a command ("Do this", "Return that"), not as a description; e.g. don't write "Returns the pathname ...".

questions.question: What separates the summary line of a multi-line docstring from the more elaborate description?
questions.evidence: Multi-line docstrings consist of a summary line just like a one-line docstring, followed by a blank line, followed by a more elaborate description.

questions.question: In a with statement, what happens to an exception raised in the block if __exit__() returns a true value?
questions.evidence: IMPORTANT: if ``mgr.__exit__()`` returns a "true" value, the exception is "swallowed".

questions.question: What arguments is __exit__() called with when the with block finishes without an exception?
questions.evidence: ``mgr.__exit__()`` is called with three ``None`` arguments.

questions.question: Which decorator turns a generator function into a context manager factory?
questions.evidence: the decorator to convert a generator function into a context manager factory is ``contextlib.contextmanager``.

questions.question: Why does the with statement raise TypeError rather than AttributeError when __enter__ or __exit__ is missing?
questions.evidence: The fact that the abstract object C API raises ``TypeError`` rather than ``AttributeError`` is an accident of history, rather than a deliberate design decision

questions.question: What is the shorthand for writing Union[T1, None] in a type hint?
questions.evidence: As a shorthand for ``Union[T1, None]`` you can write ``Optional[T1]``;

questions.question: How do you write a type hint that refers to a class that has not been defined yet?
questions.evidence: When a type hint contains names that have not been defined yet, that definition may be expressed as a string literal, to be resolved later.

questions.question: What file extension do type stub files use?
questions.evidence: While stub files are syntactically valid Python modules, they use the ``.pyi`` extension to make it possible to maintain stub files in the same directory as the corresponding real module.

questions.question: What happens if a '# type: ignore' comment is placed on a line by itself at the top of a file?
questions.evidence: A ``# type: ignore`` comment on a line by itself at the top of a file, before any docstrings, imports, or other executable code, silences all errors in the file.

questions.question: What naming convention is recommended for type variables declared with covariant=True?
questions.evidence: By convention, it is recommended to use names ending in ``_co`` for type variables defined with ``covariant=True``

questions.question: How should a type checker treat a function that has no annotations at all?
questions.evidence: Any function without annotations should be treated as having the most general type possible, or ignored, by any type checker.

questions.question: Which special type annotates a function that never returns normally, such as one that always raises?
questions.evidence: The ``typing`` module provides a special type ``NoReturn`` to annotate functions that never return normally.

questions.question: What happens if you use await outside of an async def function?
questions.evidence: It is a ``SyntaxError`` to use ``await`` outside of an ``async def`` function

questions.question: What is raised when a native coroutine is garbage collected without ever being awaited?
questions.evidence: When a *native coroutine* is garbage collected, a ``RuntimeWarning`` is raised if it was never awaited on

questions.question: Which two magic methods does an asynchronous context manager need for async with?
questions.evidence: Two new magic methods are added: ``__aenter__`` and ``__aexit__``. Both must return an *awaitable*.

questions.question: What exception must __anext__ raise to end asynchronous iteration?
questions.evidence: To stop iteration ``__anext__`` must raise a ``StopAsyncIteration`` exception.

questions.question: What does the async/await proposal call objects that have an __await__ method?
questions.evidence: Objects with ``__await__`` method are called *Future-like* objects in the rest of this PEP.

questions.question: Which type conversions can follow an expression inside an f-string?
questions.evidence: The allowed conversions are ``'!s'``, ``'!r'``, or ``'!a'``.

questions.question: How do you put a literal curly brace in the output of an f-string?
questions.evidence: Note that the correct way to have a literal brace appear in the resulting string value is to double the brace

questions.question: Why can't a lambda appear unparenthesized inside an f-string expression?
questions.evidence: The colon is interpreted as the start of the format specifier, which means the start of the lambda expression is seen and is syntactically invalid.

questions.question: When are adjacent f-strings concatenated, compared with adjacent regular strings?
questions.evidence: Regular strings are concatenated at compile time, and f-strings are concatenated at run time.

questions.question: Which protocol is used to format the value of each f-string expression?
questions.evidence: The expression is then formatted using the ``__format__`` protocol, using the format specifier as an argument.

questions.question: What informal nickname did the := operator get during discussion of assignment expressions?
questions.evidence: During discussion of this PEP, the operator became informally known as "the walrus operator".

questions.question: Where does an assignment expression inside a list comprehension bind its target?
questions.evidence: binds the target in the containing scope, honoring a ``nonlocal`` or ``global`` declaration for the target in that scope, if one exists.

questions.question: Is 'y := f(x)' valid as a standalone statement without parentheses?
questions.evidence: Unparenthesized assignment expressions are prohibited at the top level of an expression statement.

questions.question: Do assignment expressions support augmented assignment like +=, and what is the equivalent?
questions.evidence: Augmented assignment is not supported:: total += tax # Equivalent: (total := total + tax)

questions.question: How many positional arguments must a WSGI application object accept, and what are they usually called?
questions.evidence: The application object must accept two positional arguments. For the sake of illustration, we have named them ``environ`` and ``start_response``

questions.question: What are WSGI components called that act as a server to an application and as an application to a server?
questions.evidence: Note that a single object may play the role of a server with respect to some application(s), while also acting as an application with respect to some server(s). Such "middleware" components

questions.question: Through which encoding must the content of WSGI native strings be translatable to bytes?
questions.evidence: the *content* of native strings must still be translatable to bytes via the Latin-1 encoding!

questions.question: If the iterable returned by a WSGI application has a close() method, what must the server do?
questions.evidence: If the iterable returned by the application has a ``close()`` method, the server or gateway **must** call that method upon completion of the current request

questions.question: Why was the WSGI spec reissued as a new PEP instead of keeping PEP 333?
questions.evidence: This is an updated version of :pep:`333`, modified slightly to improve usability under Python 3, and to incorporate several long-standing de facto amendments to the WSGI protocol.

questions.question: Which pattern always matches but does not bind any variables?
questions.evidence: This special pattern which is written ``_`` (and called wildcard) always matches but it doesn't bind any variables.

questions.question: What restriction applies to the variables bound by the alternatives of an or pattern?
questions.evidence: An important restriction when writing or patterns is that all alternatives should bind the same variables.

questions.question: In what order are the alternatives in an or pattern tried?
questions.evidence: Patterns are tried from left to right; this may be relevant to know what is bound if more than one alternative matches.

questions.question: When is a guard on a case clause evaluated?
questions.evidence: The guard is not part of the pattern, it's part of the case. It's only checked if the pattern matches, and after all the pattern variables have been bound
